### Observed differences

- All six qualifying evidence items concern resource allocation (how the work of an activity is distributed over resources); no control-flow or timing items qualified at the configured thresholds. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- For six activities — A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22 — the resources holding the work changed markedly. In the earlier window, one group of resources held the largest individual shares on every one of these activities (for example User_18 with roughly 6–10 in 100 assignments each); in the later window that group no longer holds any reported share, while newcomers — including User_41, previously unreported — hold roughly 6–11 in 100. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- The same resources lost and gained across activities: a common group of about six resources lost share on all six activities, and two common newcomers, including User_41, gained on all six, so this reads as one reallocation affecting several activities rather than six unrelated shifts. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- On A13, A14 and A17 the redistribution also concentrated work: User_27 rose from about 5 in 100 assignments to about 18–19 in 100, becoming the largest single holder, while the unattributed "other" pool fell by about 8 in 100. On A01, A03 and A22 the shares stayed more evenly spread and the "other" pool stayed at roughly 33–45 in 100. [ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN006]
- Participation itself barely moved: the number of observations behind each profile is nearly identical in the two windows (about 200 vs 200 for A01, 331 vs 323 for A13/A14, 305 vs 304 for A17, 121 vs 127 for A22), so the difference is who performs the activities, not how often they run. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
- Each activity's assignment-profile difference has a cosine dissimilarity of 0.37–0.51 and is larger than all but about 1 in 2000 of random re-splits of the pooled data; six resource items were flagged where about 0.003 would be expected if nothing had changed. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]

### Inference

Support level: Supported hypothesis

The evidence supports the hypothesis that resource allocation changed for a set of activities: in the later window, work on A01, A03, A13, A14, A17 and A22 was reassigned from one group of resources to a largely different group (User_18's group out, User_41's group in), and on A13, A14 and A17 the work additionally became concentrated on User_27, whose share roughly quadrupled to about 19 in 100 assignments. Supporting signs: the change is measured directly on the assignment shares of each activity; all six activities move in the same direction with largely overlapping departing and arriving groups; every difference exceeds all but about 1 in 2000 random re-splits; six items were flagged in the resource family against a chance expectation of about 0.003; and participation counts are stable, so this is a reallocation of work rather than the activities running more or less often. Limitations: only the largest shares are reported per activity, so resources that dropped out may retain small unreported shares; A13 and A14 show identical profiles and may reflect one shared behaviour rather than two independent changes; and the evidence cannot rule out that a shift in the mix of cases, rather than a change in allocation rules, routed the work to different resources.

Other differences: none beyond the allocation pattern above; no control-flow or timing items qualified. [ASSIGN001, ASSIGN002, ASSIGN003, ASSIGN004, ASSIGN005, ASSIGN006]
